title: The right to sell
objectives: Draw a put option’s payoff at expiry.

screens.prose: A **put option** gives you the right to sell one share for £100.00 at expiry. As with a call, you do not have to use it. At expiry the share trades at £86.00.
screens.question: What is the put worth to you on that day?

widget.label: Value of the put at expiry

hints.text: Where could you buy the share, and what does the put let you sell it for?
Buy in the market at £86.00, then sell to the put's writer at £100.00.
$100 - 86 = 14$. The right to sell high is worth £14.00.

feedback.correct: You sell for £100.00 a share worth £86.00: £14.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the right to sell at £100.00, buying the share at its market price.

byKey.call-sum: You worked out $S_T - K$, the call's sum. A put gains when the share ends below the strike.
byKey.share: You counted the whole share. The put pays the gap between £100.00 and £86.00.
byKey.nothing: You expected the fall to hurt. A fall is exactly what a put pays for.

explain.text: The put lets you sell at £100.00 a share the market values at £86.00. So the put is worth £14.00 on that day. Every £1.00 lower would add £1.00.

screens.prose: Slide the price at expiry across the whole axis, from £0.00 to £140.00. Watch the label on the dot.
screens.question: What is the most this put can ever pay?

options.text: £100.00, when the share ends at £0.00
There is no limit
options.why: You read the put like a call. A share price cannot fall below £0.00, so the payoff stops at £100.00.

options.text: £140.00, at the right end of the axis
options.why: You read the right end of the price axis. The put pays most at the left end, where the share is worthless.

options.text: £50.00, half the strike
options.why: You stopped part way. Slide all the way to £0.00 and read the label.

feedback.correct: At most £100.00, the strike, if the share becomes worthless.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the price all the way to the left.

explain.text: The put pays more the lower the share ends, but a share cannot fall below £0.00. There the put sells a worthless share for £100.00. So its payoff is capped at the strike $K$.

screens.prose: The words carry over from calls: strike $K$, expiry, price at expiry $S_T$, exercise. A put is **in the money** at expiry when $S_T < K$. Drag the diamond to move the strike.
screens.question: Drag the strike so that the put pays £6.00 when the share ends at £88.00.

hints.text: A put pays $K - S_T$ when the share ends below the strike.
The strike has to sit £6.00 above the price at expiry.
$K - 88 = 6$ gives $K = 94$. Drag the diamond to £94.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The put pays the gap from the share price up to the strike.

byKey.call-way: You put the strike below the share price, as for a call. Then the put would pay nothing.
byKey.p1: The strike is not yet £6.00 above £88.00. Read the gap between the dashed line and the diamond.

explain.text: With $K = 94$ the put pays $K - S_T = 94 - 88 = 6$. The put's line is the call's picture in a mirror. It slopes down to the left of the strike and is flat to the right.

screens.prose: A put struck at $K = \text{£}50.00$. For each price at expiry, decide whether you would sell at £50.00.
screens.question: Fill in the put's payoff at each price at expiry.

hints.text: Below the strike you sell at £50.00; above it you keep your right unused.
At £55.00, selling for £50.00 would lose £5.00, so you do not.
$50 - 30 = 20$ and $50 - 42 = 8$. At £50.00 and above the put pays 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pay $50 - S_T$ below the strike and 0 at or above it.

byKey.r3c1: At £55.00 you would not sell for £50.00. The put pays 0, not −5.
byKey.r4c1: At £70.00 you would not sell for £50.00. The put pays 0, not −20.
byKey.r2c1: At the strike, selling for £50.00 a share worth £50.00 gains nothing.
byKey.r0c1: At £30.00 you sell for £50.00 a share worth £30.00.
byKey.r1c1: At £42.00 you sell for £50.00 a share worth £42.00.

explain.text: Below £50.00 the put pays $50 - S_T$, rising £1.00 for every £1.00 the share falls. At or above the strike it pays 0, and never less. The floor is the right not to exercise.

screens.prose: Two edge cases. A put struck at £0.00 is a right to sell for nothing. A company that goes bust leaves its share at £0.00.
screens.question: Fill in each payoff at expiry.

hints.text: Use $\max(K - S_T, 0)$ with each strike.
With $K = 0$, $K - S_T$ is never positive.
$\max(0 - 37, 0) = 0$ and $\max(0 - 0, 0) = 0$. A bust company gives $\max(60 - 0, 0) = 60$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $K - S_T$ in each row and keep it only if it is positive.

byKey.r0c2: A right to sell for £0.00 is never worth using, so it pays 0.
byKey.r1c2: Selling a worthless share for £0.00 gains nothing.
byKey.r2c2: The share is worthless and the put sells it for £60.00: the full strike.

explain.text: A put struck at £0.00 can never pay, so it is worthless. A put on a share that ends at £0.00 pays its whole strike. That is the largest payoff any put can have.

screens.prose: Last lesson you sorted three calls on a share at £104.00. Here are three **puts** with the same strikes. The words mean the same: in the money if exercising today would pay.

state.caption: Three puts on one share, three strikes

screens.question: Place each label on its put.

hints.text: Would selling at the strike today beat the £104.00 market price?
Only one strike sits above today's price.
Selling at £110.00 beats £104.00: in the money. Selling at £95.00 loses: out of the money.

feedback.correct: 95 out, 104 at, 110 in: the reverse of the calls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For a put, ask whether selling at the strike beats today's £104.00.

byKey.otm: You copied the calls. A put struck at £95.00 sells below the £104.00 market price, so it is out of the money.
byKey.itm: You copied the calls. The put that pays today is the one struck above £104.00.
byKey.atm: At the money means the strike equals today's price, £104.00.

explain.text: A put gains from a strike above the price, so the 110 put is in the money by £6.00. The 95 put is out of the money. For the same strikes, calls and puts swap labels.

screens.prose: Whoever sells you a call must sell you the share if you exercise. Their side is a **short call**. A colleague says a long put and a short call are the same bet on a fall. The share ends at £130.00.

state.caption: Top: you own a put. Bottom: you sold someone a call. Both struck at £100.00.

screens.question: What do the long put and the short call pay at £130.00?

options.text: Long put £0.00; short call −£30.00

options.why: You drew the put as a falling line with no floor. The put's owner simply does not sell at £100.00, so it pays £0.00.

options.text: Both £0.00
options.why: You gave the short call a floor. The seller has no choice: they must hand over a £130.00 share for £100.00.

options.text: Long put −£30.00; short call £0.00
options.why: You swapped the two. The one with a choice, the put's owner, is the one who cannot lose here.

hints.text: Who has a choice at expiry: the put's owner, or the call's seller?
Read each line at £130.00.
The put owner walks away: 0. The call seller must sell at £100.00 a share worth £130.00: −30.

feedback.correct: The put owner walks away; the call seller pays £30.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The owner of an option has a choice; the seller does not.

byKey.both-neg: You drew the put without its floor. A long put never pays less than 0.
byKey.both-zero: You gave the seller the buyer's choice. The short call must deliver.

explain.text: Both positions like a fall, but only the put has a floor. The put owner chooses, so their worst payoff is 0. The call seller has no choice, so a rise costs them without limit.

screens.prose: You found the put's payoff the same way as the call's: exercise if it pays, else walk away. $$\text{put payoff} = \max(K - S_T,\ 0).$$ It is the call's formula with $S_T$ and $K$ swapped, which mirrors the picture about the strike.
screens.question: Why can a put never pay more than its strike $K$?

options.text: Because $S_T$ cannot be below 0, so $K - S_T$ is at most $K$
Because the writer caps the payoff in the contract
options.why: You looked for a rule in the contract. The cap comes from the share price, which cannot go negative.

options.text: Because the max stops it
options.why: You read the max as a ceiling. It sets a floor at 0; the ceiling comes from $S_T \ge 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how low $S_T$ can go.

explain.text: The payoff $K - S_T$ grows as $S_T$ falls, and $S_T$ stops at 0. So the largest payoff is $K - 0 = K$. A call has no such cap, since $S_T$ can rise without limit.

screens.prose: You own a share bought at £100.00. To insure it, you buy a put struck at £90.00. The bold line is the share and the put together, against the £100.00 you paid. Ignore the put's price for now.
screens.question: The share falls to £70.00. What is your gain on the share and the put together?

widget.label: Gain on share and put
widget.accept: −£10.00: −£30.00 on the share, +£20.00 from the put

hints.text: Add the gain on the share to the put's payoff.
The share loses £30.00; the put struck at £90.00 pays £20.00.

feedback.correct: −£30.00 on the share, +£20.00 from the put: −£10.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the share's gain and the put's payoff.

byKey.no-put: That is the share alone. The put pays £20.00 at £70.00.
byKey.put-only: That is the put alone. You also lost £30.00 on the share.
byKey.to-strike: You assumed the put restores the whole £100.00. It sells at £90.00, so £10.00 is still lost.

explain.text: Below £90.00 every £1.00 the share loses, the put pays back. So the loss stops at £10.00, however far the share falls. That is why a put is insurance; level 2 adds its cost.

screens.prose: A fund holds a share at £100.00. Results are announced next week, and a fall would hurt. The fund buys puts struck at £95.00 that expire after the announcement.
screens.question: Fill in what each put pays at expiry.

hints.text: Compare each price with the £95.00 strike.
Only one of the two prices is below the strike.

feedback.correct: £7.00 after bad news, £0.00 after good news.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\max(95 - S_T, 0)$ for each price.

byKey.r0c1: At £88.00 the put sells for £95.00 a share worth £88.00.
byKey.r1c1: At £101.00 the fund would not sell for £95.00. The put pays 0, not −6.

explain.text: After bad news the put pays £7.00 per share, which offsets part of the £12.00 fall. After good news it pays nothing, and the fund keeps the rise. The first £5.00 of any fall is not covered.

ideas: A put is the right, not the duty, to sell at the strike $K$ at expiry.
Its payoff falls with slope −1 down to the strike and is flat at 0 above it: the call's picture mirrored.
The most a put can pay is $K$, when the share ends at 0. That makes a put insurance for a holding.
summary.trap: A long put has a floor at 0; a short call does not. Both like a fall, but only the put's owner can walk away.

quiz.prose: A put is struck at £40.00. At expiry the share is at £31.25.
quiz.question: What does the put pay?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A put pays the strike minus the price when that is positive.

byKey.neg: You used $S_T - K$, the call's sum. A put pays $K - S_T$.
byKey.share: That is the share price, not the payoff.

explain.text: The share ends below the strike, so the put is exercised: $\max(40 - 31.25, 0) = 8.75$.

quiz.prose: A put on a bank's shares is struck at £120.00.
quiz.question: What is the largest payoff the put can ever have?

options.text: £120.00, if the bank goes bust
There is no largest payoff
options.why: You treated the put like a call. The share cannot fall below £0.00.
That is the smallest payoff, when the share ends at or above £120.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How low can the share price go?

explain.text: $\max(120 - S_T, 0)$ is largest when $S_T$ is smallest, which is 0. So the most the put pays is £120.00.

quiz.prose: A share trades at £60.00. There is a call and a put, both struck at £65.00.
quiz.question: Which statement is true today?

options.text: The put is in the money by £5.00; the call is out of the money
The call is in the money by £5.00; the put is out of the money
options.why: You used the call rule for both. A call needs the price above the strike.

options.text: Both are in the money by £5.00
options.why: Only one side of a £5.00 gap can pay. Exercising the call would buy at £65.00 a share worth £60.00.

options.text: Neither, since the share is at neither strike
options.why: In the money needs only that exercising pays, not that the price sits at the strike.

feedback.correct: Selling at £65.00 beats £60.00: the put pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which exercise would pay today.

explain.text: Exercising the put sells at £65.00 a share worth £60.00, a gain of £5.00. Exercising the call would buy it at £65.00, a loss, so the call is out of the money.

quiz.prose: Four descriptions of a payoff diagram at expiry, against the share price.
quiz.question: Which one is a long put struck at £80.00?

options.text: Falls with slope −1 down to 0 at £80.00, then flat at 0
A straight line falling with slope −1 through 0 at £80.00
options.why: You left out the floor. Above £80.00 the owner walks away, so the payoff is 0, not negative.

options.text: Flat at 0 up to £80.00, then rising with slope 1
options.why: That is a long call. A put pays for falls, to the left of the strike.

options.text: Flat at 0 up to £80.00, then falling with slope −1
options.why: That is the seller of a call. A long put is flat on the right, not the left.

feedback.correct: Down to the strike, then flat.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does a put pay, and where does it pay nothing?

explain.text: Below £80.00 the put pays $80 - S_T$, which shrinks as $S_T$ rises. At and above £80.00 it pays 0. That is a falling line that meets a floor at the strike.
